content.body: Have you ever tried to count all the unique items in a shopping cart? In this lesson, we'll learn how to count subarrays with exactly K distinct elements. This is a common pattern in data analysis and string processing.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain what makes a subarray have exactly K distinct elements
2. Implement a solution using the sliding window technique
3. Use a hash map to track element frequencies
4. Count valid subarrays efficiently in one pass
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. Look at this array:
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: How many subarrays have exactly 2 distinct elements?
content.successMessage: Great! You found that [1,2], [2,1], and [1,2,1] all have exactly 2 distinct elements.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now with 5 elements, how many subarrays have exactly 2 distinct elements?
content.successMessage: Excellent! You manually counted subarrays like [1,2], [2,1], [1,2,1], and many more.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: How many subarrays have exactly 3 distinct elements in this array?
content.successMessage: Well done! You checked many combinations to find all subarrays with exactly 3 unique elements.

content.body: What you just did was brute force: you looked at every possible subarray and counted distinct elements for each one. For small arrays, this works, but it becomes very slow for larger data.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 1000 elements, there are over 500,000 possible subarrays! Checking each one separately would be extremely slow. We need a smarter approach. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. We can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to remember which elements we've seen and how many times they appear. This lets us track distinct counts without rescanning the entire subarray each time.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. Each time we add or remove an element from our window, we update our notebook.

content.body: We'll use a sliding window with two pointers and a frequency map. The key insight: subarrays with exactly K distinct elements = (subarrays with at most K distinct) - (subarrays with at most K-1 distinct).
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For array [1,2,1,2,3], K=2:
1. Count subarrays with ≤2 distinct: expand window while distinct ≤2, count all subarrays
2. Count subarrays with ≤1 distinct: same process
3. Subtract: (≤2) - (≤1) = exactly 2 distinct
We use a frequency map to track counts efficiently.

content.body:
Here's our plan:
1. Create a helper function that counts subarrays with at most K distinct elements
2. Use two pointers (left and right) to define our window
3. Maintain a frequency map to track element counts in the window
4. Expand the right pointer, updating the map
5. When we have more than K distinct, shrink from the left
6. Count valid subarrays as we go
7. Use the formula: exactly K = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the helper function skeleton
steps.instruction: Let's start by creating the helper function that counts subarrays with at most K distinct elements. Create a function called atMostK with parameters nums and k.

steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function called atMostK(nums, k).

steps.title: Initialize variables
steps.instruction: Inside atMostK, initialize the variables we'll need: left pointer at 0, result counter at 0, and an empty frequency map.
steps.hint: Use let for variables that will change, and {} for an empty object as our frequency map.
steps.expectedOutcome: Variables left, result, and freq initialized
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've set up our tracking variables.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Don't forget to initialize left, result, and freq.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need three variables: left starting at 0, result at 0, and freq as an empty object.

steps.title: Set up the main loop
steps.instruction: Now add a for loop that iterates through nums with a right pointer. We'll use this to expand our window.
steps.hint: Use a standard for loop with right as the index variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: A for loop that iterates through nums
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The loop will let us process each element as we expand our window.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your loop goes through all elements of nums.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need a for loop like: for (let right = 0; right < nums.length; right++)

steps.title: Update frequency map
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, update the frequency map for the current element nums[right]. If it doesn't exist in freq, initialize it to 0, then increment.
steps.hint: Check if freq[nums[right]] exists, then increment it.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that updates freq for the current element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we're tracking how many times each element appears in our window.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure you handle the case when the element isn't in freq yet.

steps.title: Shrink window when needed
steps.instruction: After updating freq, check if we have more than k distinct elements. If so, move left pointer forward and update freq until we're back to ≤k distinct.
steps.hint: Use a while loop that checks Object.keys(freq).length > k
steps.expectedOutcome: While loop that shrinks window when distinct count > k
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! This keeps our window valid with at most k distinct elements.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good! Remember to decrement freq and remove elements that reach 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: while (Object.keys(freq).length > k) { decrement freq[nums[left]], remove if 0, left++ }

steps.title: Count valid subarrays
steps.instruction: After the while loop, count all subarrays ending at right that have at most k distinct. Add this to result, then return result at the end.
steps.hint: The number of valid subarrays ending at right is (right - left + 1).
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that updates result and returns it
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we're counting all valid subarrays efficiently.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Don't forget to update result and return it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: result += right - left + 1; inside the loop, and return result; at the end.

steps.title: Complete the main function
steps.instruction: Now create the main function subarraysWithKDistinct that uses our helper. It should return atMostK(nums, k) - atMostK(nums, k-1).
steps.hint: Make sure to handle the case when k is 0 or 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented the complete solution using the sliding window and frequency map pattern.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good work! Make sure your main function returns the difference correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: function subarraysWithKDistinct(nums, k) { return atMostK(nums, k) - atMostK(nums, k-1); }

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned how to count subarrays with exactly K distinct elements using the sliding window technique and frequency maps. Remember: the key insight is converting 'exactly K' to 'at most K minus at most K-1'. This pattern of using a lookup structure to remember what we've seen appears in many array and string problems. Keep practicing with different values of K to build your intuition!
